argument: Building on Kant's split between the phenomenal and noumenal worlds, the episode argues that even total scientific knowledge would only ever amount to total knowledge of human experience, never of things as they truly are, because our minds and senses are an evolved 'experience machine' built for survival, not for perceiving ultimate reality. Kant uses this limit to demolish traditional proofs of God (the ontological and cosmological arguments) while still leaving room for faith in God, souls, and free will as legitimate, since these lie permanently beyond what any human apparatus could ever know. The episode closes by asking whether knowledge itself is really the end goal people are after, or just a bridge to something else.
keyIdeas: Kant distinguishes truth from knowledge: even a Laplace-style total knowledge of every atom's location would still only be total knowledge of human experience, not of the noumenal 'things in themselves.'
What our mind and senses produce is described as a 'crude map' of the noumenal world — a limited, practical representation built for navigation, not a picture of reality itself.
The post-apocalyptic WIFI-signal example shows that what we can and can't perceive is an arbitrary product of what happened to aid survival, not evidence of everything that actually exists.

Kant debunks Anselm's ontological argument and, agreeing with Hume, treats the cosmological 'prime mover' argument's assumption that the universe needed a cause as a feature of how our minds organize experience rather than a fact about reality itself.

Kant distinguishes superstitious faith (belief about something that could in principle be investigated and known) from legitimate faith (belief about something permanently unknowable to the human mind), illustrated by tribespeople blaming volcanic eruptions on human sacrifice.

terms.def: The world of things as they truly are, in themselves, permanently beyond direct human access.
The world of appearances that our mind and senses construct — a practical, limited 'map' of the noumenal world, not reality itself.
The episode's term for the human mind and senses as an apparatus built to depict whatever is useful for survival, not to perceive things in themselves.
Anselm's proof that God, as 'that than which nothing greater can be conceived,' must exist because existing is greater than not existing; Kant debunks it.
Kant's distinction: faith about something knowable through investigation is superstition, while faith about something permanently unknowable to us is legitimate.
